catalog_quote: The Quechua spoken in Arequipa belongs to the Cuzco-Bolivia variety. Unfortunately, the literature describing Arequipa Quechua is very scant, indeed, and one must therefore rely for insight on the far more extensive analyses of the varieties spoken in Cuzco, Puno, and Bolivia. Quechua is an agglutinative language, with morphologically complex words constructed exclusively through suffixation. Each suffix usually consists of one or two syllables corresponding to a single morpheme, with word stress on the penultimate syllable. [p. 47] ... Since Quechua word stress falls on the penultimate syllable, by Slobin's formula, all syllables are perceptually prominent; that is, depending on the verb form, all syllables in one verb or another achieve perceptual salience by virtue of having primary stress or occurring in initial/final position. [p. 91] ... Since they invariably occur in word-final position, they never have primary word stress. (The reader will recall that Quechua words generally bear stress on the penultimate syllable.) [p. 240] || Adelaar & Muysken 2004: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. [p. 206]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.quote: The Quechua spoken in Arequipa belongs to the Cuzco-Bolivia variety. Unfortunately, the literature describing Arequipa Quechua is very scant, indeed [...] Quechua is an agglutinative language, with morphologically complex words constructed exclusively through suffixation. Each suffix usually consists of one or two syllables corresponding to a single morpheme, with word stress on the penultimate syllable. [p. 58:] Since these suffixes [the evidential enclitics -mi/-n, -chá, -cha, -s(i), -chu] always occur in word-final position, none but "Speculative" /-chá/ is ever phonologically stressed.

Unfortunately, the literature describing Arequipa Quechua is very scant, indeed, and one must therefore rely for insight on the far more extensive analyses of the varieties spoken in Cuzco, Puno, and Bolivia.[fn 9] Quechua is an agglutinative language, with morphologically complex words constructed exclusively through suffixation. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (suffixed) word, so stress moves rightward as suffixes are added (e.g. maqa-wá-nki); word-final enclitics are therefore unstressed, except the 'speculative' enclitic -chá, which carries (final) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final 'Speculative' enclitic /-chá/ is stressed (final stress); the 1999 ILV La Unión writing guide (p. 14) likewise marks final stress with a tilde only on 'algunas enfáticas: hamuyyá, pichá, manamá, arí, mamáy, awiláy'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (morphological word including suffixes); author's footnote 9 says the chapter is 'based on personal observation, as well as information gleaned from' published grammars of Cuzco, Puno and Bolivian Quechua, so the stress statement is first-hand for Chalhuanca (Caylloma, Arequipa) speech but phrased pan-Southern-Quechua; no instrumental data, no citation forms vs phrase distinction.
new_statements.identity_note: Courtney 1998 describes the Quechua of Chalhuanca (district Yanque, province Caylloma, dept. Arequipa), which she herself assigns to the 'Cuzco-Bolivia variety'; Glottolog files this thesis under areq1237 and SIL's archive files the Caylloma papers (Kindberg 1989) under qxu ('Highland/Northern Arequipa' dialects), but the core of qxu/areq1237 is La Unión province (Cotahuasi; Glottolog dialect cota1243), whose speech the 1987 ILV guide shows differs (La Unión puri-cha-ni vs Chivay/Caylloma puri-sha-ni, Cabanaconde puri-chha-ni) and which Glottolog classes as Ayacuchan. The only La Unión-specific items read (Buckingham 1992; ILV 1999 Runasimita Qillqasun p. 14) are consistent (tilde only on final-stressed emphatics) but do not state the default rule. If the catalog keys strictly to Cotahuasi/La Unión, treat Courtney as adjacent-dialect (Caylloma, arguably cusc1236) evidence.

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyl- labic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimita- tion. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alalaw 'how cold!'. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junin word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable. [p. 206] ... In Pacaraos Quechua (see section 3.2.9) stress is phonemic. It may lie either on the penultimate or on the final syllable. [...] Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns, involving word-initial stress and stress dependent on syllable structure, are found in QI Ancash and in QI Cajatambo (cf. Torero 1964: 461; Parker 1976). [p. 207]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Courtney 1998 statement (penultimate), but at the level of 'most Quechua dialects' rather than Arequipa-La Unión specifically; adds the emphatic/interjection final-stress exception, which matches the ILV 1999 Runasimita Qillqasun tilde-only-on-emphatic-final-stress note already; Identity: p. 187 puts the Arequipa provinces of Caravelí, Condesuyos and La Unión under Ayacucho Quechua and the provinces of Arequipa, Castilla, Caylloma and Condesuyos under Cuzco Quechua.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-wide statement: in most Quechua dialects stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word, and this serves as a word-delimitation cue. The book gives no stress statement specific to Arequipa or La Unión Quechua; the named exceptions (phonemic final/penultimate contrast in Pacaraos, word-initial and weight-dependent patterns in quantity-insensitive Ancash and Cajatambo, final stress from syllable elision in Tarma and northern Junín) all concern Quechua I or Pacaraos, none the Arequipa varieties, which the book assigns to Quechua IIC (Ayacucho and Cuzco Quechua).
new_statements.exceptions: Interjections and emphatic expressions may carry word-final stress (alalaw 'how cold!'); word-final stress from elision of a final syllable in Tarma and northern Junín; Pacaraos has phonemic final vs penultimate stress (final stress with the first-person marker -'y and elided suffixes); quantity-insensitive Ancash and Cajatambo have word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent patterns; Huaraz stress pattern described by Torero 1964 in terms of long (CVC, CV:) vs short (CV) syllables; footnote 24: whether an Ancash-type accentuation reflects Proto-Quechua is debated.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken 2004 p. 187 split the department of Arequipa between two Quechua IIC dialects: 'Ayacucho Quechua covers.. Arequipa (provinces of Caraveli, Condesuyos and La Union)' and 'Cuzco Quechua includes.. Arequipa (provinces of Arequipa, Castilla, Caylloma and Condesuyos)'. So the La Unión (Cotahuasi) part of Glottolog's areq1237 is Ayacucho-type and the Caylloma/Castilla part Cuzco-type in their scheme; Courtney 1998's field site (Chalhuanca, Caylloma) is on the Cuzco side. The book has no stress statement for either Arequipa variety; only the family-wide penultimate rule applies. They also note (p. 175) that the upper Colca basin (Caylloma) was once Aymara-speaking and is 'entirely Quechuanised today', and that glottalised/aspirated consonants in Cuzco, Puno, Arequipa and Bolivian Quechua are generally attributed to Aymaran diffusion.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (Courtney 1998: penultimate) and identical to the existing Adelaar & Muysken statement held by the project, which was assembled from archive.org FTS snippets; the full born-digital page now confirms that snippet transcript verbatim and its page assignment (the 'most Quechua dialects' paragraph and examples (34)-(35) are on p. 206; Pacaraos onward is p. 207). The statement is family-level ('most Quechua dialects'), applied to Arequipa via the p. 187 classification, not an Arequipa-specific description; the emphatic final-stress exception matches the ILV 1999 Runasimita Qillqasun tilde note already
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel (syllable) of every polysyllabic word in most Quechua dialects, which by the book's own dialect geography (p. 187) includes the Arequipa varieties (Ayacucho Quechua in Caravelí, Condesuyos, La Unión; Cuzco Quechua in Arequipa, Castilla, Caylloma, Condesuyos); the only exception stated for these dialects is word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alaláw). The non-penultimate systems the book lists are all elsewhere (Pacaraos phonemic penult/final; quantity-insensitive Ancash, Cajatambo weight/initial; QIIA Ferreñafe, QIIB Amazonas/Chachapoyas initial; Tarma/northern Junín final by elision; quantity-insensitive final stress on the word-final first-person long vowel). No Arequipa-specific stress sentence exists in the book (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text: Arequipa is mentioned for glottalised/aspirated stops p. 35/195/199, dialect geography p. 187, Aymara substratum p. 262, never with stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said about secondary stress for Quechua II/southern Quechua (the phrase 'secondary stress' does not occur in the Quechua chapter).
new_statements.exceptions: interjections and emphatic expressions may carry word-final stress (alaláw 'how cold!'); other exceptions listed (Tarma/northern Junín elision, quantity-insensitive first-person long vowel, Pacaraos phonemic stress, Ancash/Cajatambo weight-sensitive, Ferreñafe/Amazonas initial) concern other dialects, not Arequipa.
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken 2004 do not treat Arequipa Quechua as a unit: p. 187 (after Chirinos Rivera 1998) assigns the Arequipa provinces of Caravelí, Condesuyos and La Unión to Ayacucho Quechua (QIIC, no glottalised/aspirated stops) and the provinces of Arequipa, Castilla, Caylloma and Condesuyos to Cuzco Quechua (QIIC with laryngealised stops; Arequipa and Puno subdialects show Aymara lexical/morphological borrowing, pp. 187, 199, 262). The stress statement is generic to 'most Quechua dialects'; Courtney 1998 (the catalog source) describes Caylloma (Chalhuanca, Yanque), i.e. the Cuzco-type part.
